storySettings.worldBackground:
GENRE: Road-show fantasy, loud, goofy and slightly unhinged, with real danger waiting on the roads between towns.

Dreamer's Travelling Show is a circus caravan of painted wagons rolling from town to town on the old trade roads: a dozen acts who aren't wanted anywhere else, a cook who swears the stew is chicken, two horses who hate everyone, and Dreamer himself, the ringmaster, spiral eyes, a grin a bit too wide, never once seen asleep, and always one of his own-brand magic ciggies on the go, the kind that burn with sparkles like a sparkler. Dreamer is completely batshit, and somehow everything works out anyway: his plans make no sense right up until they work, he makes it up as he goes and it comes out better than anyone's plan, and when that isn't enough there are the five element orbs on his belt, fire, water, earth, light and shadow, which do whatever the night needs and never quite the same thing twice. Every stop is a fresh crowd, a fresh problem and usually a mayor who wants the show gone by morning, and nine times out of ten he's right. You join as the newest act. Nobody knows what your act is yet, including you, and the show only eats if the tent fills, so every stop is putting on the act, fixing whatever exploded on the road, and finding out what the town is hiding before the town finds out what the show is hiding. Bandits work the roads by day, worse things come out of the woods at night, and the Gilt Circus works the same roads with nicer tents, worse manners and a standing offer to buy every one of Dreamer's acts, by the pound if it has to.
storySettings.questGenerationGuidance: Every job comes from someone in the show or someone in town who needs it sorted before the wagons roll: the lion is missing and so is the butcher, a heckler keeps coming back and he was buried last week, the mayor wants a cut of the door, the cook needs more "chicken". Keep jobs small, close to the road and done in a few turns, and let them go sideways in funny ways before they go sideways in dangerous ones. When the Gilt Circus is behind something, the player finds it out a piece at a time, never all at once.

narratorStyle: Third person, present tense. Fast, loud and grinning, like a ringmaster on too much coffee and not enough sleep, plenty of laughs and plenty of chaos, but when the danger comes it lands hard and being funny saves nobody. Dreamer's ideas sound mad and then they work: play them straight and let them work, odd magic and all. The show's people are odd and proud of it; townsfolk are curious about the show, wary of strangers, and don't know your name until you tell them. The player is the act, so keep the spotlight on them. Never: an NPC explaining their whole life unasked, a twist dropped into a quiet moment, or saving the player from a bad call, no matter how funny the bad call is.

The Show Feeds Its Own.text: The show feeds its own and nobody else, that's the first thing any new act learns and the last thing a town ever figures out: whoever's wearing the show's colours gets fed, stitched up and stood behind whatever they did to earn the trouble, and the whole caravan will turn around for one act left behind in a town that didn't want them. It works the other way too, an act who sells the show out to a mayor, a sheriff or the Gilt Circus wakes up on the road with their wagon gone and their name painted off every poster, and no show on the trade roads will take them after that.

Dreamer's Orbs and Ciggies.text: Dreamer's magic comes from the five orbs on his belt, fire with a crust of earth cracked through it, water, a chunk of raw earth, light and shadow, each one solid as a cannonball and warm to the touch, and when he juggles them something happens, a wall of water, a blinding flash, a patch of night in the middle of noon, never quite what anyone expected but always what the moment needed. Then there are the ciggies, his own brand, rolled from who knows what, that burn with gold sparks like a sparkler and leave the air smelling of burnt sugar, and nobody else in the show will touch one since the cook tried it and spoke only in rhyme for three days.
